Investigating why the application auto-reloads when using ngrok.

The `mcpServer` flag in `next.config.ts` is disabled. The `allowedDevOrigins` list includes ngrok domains. This triggers frequent compilation cycles and page reloads.

A comment in the config mentions MCP logs retriggering full page reloads. I will read the systematic debugging skill and examine the code to pinpoint the exact trigger.

The terminal logs show a constant "✓ Compiled" cycle after every request. This pattern likely triggers HMR through frequent GET and POST requests to `/`, `/obs`, and `/api/obs/link`. I will check `live-studio.tsx` for polling logic that could drive these reloads.

HMR websockets likely fail through ngrok, forcing full reloads. The dev server may treat ngrok as a cross-origin origin and reload. Other suspects include ngrok interstitials, file watcher resets, and polling endpoints invalidating the router.

Next.js 15+ introduced `allowedDevOrigins` to prevent ngrok-hosted requests from triggering reload loops. Next.js 16 has a known HMR client bug where the browser connects to the wrong host, or cross-origin warnings force reloads. I will inspect the code and logs to confirm the exact trigger.
</details></think>

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
Looking into why the page auto-reloads when accessed through ngrok.

This is a known Next.js dev server issue with ngrok. The logs show constant recompilation on every request. The browser error suggests the router initializes too late. Turbopack likely triggers rebuilds on file changes.

The `mcpServer` setting was already disabled to prevent `.next/dev` log rewrites from triggering reloads. Still, constant compilation points to a file watcher loop. The HMR WebSocket injected by Next.js is another suspected culprit for ngrok connections.

ngrok's free tier injects an interstitial page and extra headers. This can break the HMR websocket connection. When the websocket drops, Next.js falls back to a full page reload. The ngrok browser warning page may also trigger these failures.

Next.js 15+ enforces cross-origin dev restrictions. If the page loads from the ngrok hostname but assets or HMR report a different origin, Next.js forces a full reload.

The ngrok host is already in `allowedDevOrigins`, so cross-origin blocking is unlikely. The real problem is Turbopack invalidating its module graph on every request. Something is writing to `.next` and forcing constant recompilation even during simple GET requests. I should check the live-studio and obs-viewer components for polling or forced reload logic.

Fast Refresh falls back to a full browser reload whenever the root layout or a server component changes, or when HMR cannot apply the update. The log pattern confirms a compile loop where Next.js writes request logs, which Turbopack then detects as a file change and rebuilds.

The `.next/dev/trace` file is being written on every request. This could be triggering Turbopack to rebuild. Another likely cause is ngrok changing the Host header. Next.js dev HMR connects via `window.location`. A changed Host header breaks the websocket connection and forces a full reload.

The HMR client retries the websocket connection. After repeated failures, it falls back to a full reload. This explains the constant page refreshes.

The ngrok interstitial HTML may be intercepting the HMR websocket upgrade. Next.js then sees a broken connection and reloads. The `x-forwarded-host` header could also make Next.js treat each request as a new origin. Since the host is already in `allowedDevOrigins`, the cross-origin block is probably not the cause. The logs still show continuous compiles and page GETs after restart.

The browser appears to be caught in a reload loop rather than just an HMR websocket failure. I will inspect the live-studio component for background polling or navigation timers that could force reloads. I also plan to review the Next.js documentation on allowedDevOrigins and HMR client behavior.
</details></think>

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
A reload loop is occurring. GET requests to "/" and "/obs" are firing constantly. The "Compiled" event keeps triggering.

These are full page reloads, not API polls. The Next.js dev HMR client is likely failing its websocket connection and forcing reloads. This is a classic Next.js dev HMR plus proxy issue.

Next.js derives the HMR websocket URL from the current page address. When using ngrok, the browser connects back to the public ngrok domain instead of localhost. The ngrok free tier likely blocks or interferes with that websocket connection, forcing the HMR client to fall back to full page reloads.

The constant "Compiled" messages reveal the root cause. The dev MCP log is rewritten on every compile. This invalidates the compile cache and forces full page reloads. Server components and next.config changes cannot use fast refresh. The code comment already notes this retriggering.

Disabling mcpServer did not stop the compiles. Another file is being rewritten on every request. The `.next/dev/trace` file is the prime suspect. Next.js writes this on every request. If the file watcher tracks it, each request triggers a recompile, which writes the trace again, creating a loop. The trace file should normally be ignored. The ngrok-specific trigger remains unclear.

Localhost works fine, so a general file-watch loop is unlikely. The issue is isolated to the HMR websocket path that only exists when the browser origin is the ngrok host. Next.js treats cross-origin dev requests as blocked unless the host is listed in `allowedDevOrigins`. This explains why the reload loop only appears behind ngrok.

The host is already in allowedDevOrigins, so the reload loop is not caused by a missing origin entry. The cause is likely a websocket origin mismatch, or ngrok's interstitial requests altering the host header. I will check the Next.js source to confirm how allowedDevOrigins interacts with HMR reloads.

The reload comes from the Next.js dev hot-reload client, which only runs while `pnpm dev` is up. The studio and OBS pages do not reload themselves.

In development, the page opens a WebSocket to `/_next/hmr` on whatever host you loaded. On localhost that socket stays on this machine. Through ngrok it is `wss://timid-flint-mutt.ngrok-free.dev/_next/hmr`. The tunnel accepts that connection (it upgrades with status 101), then drops or delays it. When the socket comes back, Next.js treats it as a restarted dev server and calls a full page reload.

The same hop also makes the dev JavaScript chunks arrive late. If one of those chunks fails, the dev runtime throws a `ChunkLoadError` and reloads again. That reload makes Turbopack compile again, which changes the chunks, so the next load can fail the same way. The server log is that loop: `Compiled`, then a fresh `GET /` and `GET /obs`, then every chunk again.

`allowedDevOrigins` already includes this ngrok host, so Next.js is not blocking the page. A production server (`pnpm start`) does not include this hot-reload client, so the tunnel would not reload the page.

_**Agent (default)**_

The phone only has to be the camera. OBS can keep showing the AI video from the computer. These options skip the ngrok dev page, so it will not keep reloading.

**1. Turn the phone into a webcam on the PC.** This is the simplest match for this app. Install a webcam app on the phone and on the computer, then connect them over USB or the same Wi-Fi. In the studio at `http://localhost:3000`, pick that camera from the dropdown and press **Start live**. Leave the OBS Browser Source on `http://localhost:3000/obs?key=zam`.

- iPhone: Camo, or Continuity Camera if the computer is a Mac
- Android: Iriun, DroidCam, or Camo

USB is steadier than Wi-Fi. The phone screen has to stay on and the app has to stay in the foreground.

**2. Keep ngrok, but run the built app.** The reload comes from the development hot-reload client. `pnpm build` and then `pnpm start` still serve port 3000, and that build has no hot reload. Open the studio on the phone at `https://timid-flint-mutt.ngrok-free.dev`, allow the camera, and press **Start live**. Add that exact origin to `APP_ORIGINS` in `.env`. OBS can stay on the localhost `/obs` link.

**3. Put the phone in OBS, then send OBS back into the studio.** Add the phone in OBS with a webcam app, NDI, or a browser source. Start **OBS Virtual Camera**. In the studio on the computer, choose **OBS Virtual Camera** as the camera and press **Start live**. The AI picture is a second OBS source: the `/obs` browser page. The raw phone and the AI video stay separate sources.

The first option keeps the studio and OBS on the computer and only uses the phone as the camera.
